parole.significato: To make familiar by use; to cause to accept; to habituate, familiarize, or inure.
parole.testo: The verb is from Middle English accustomen, from Old French acoustumer, acustumer (Modern French accoutumer) corresponding to a (“to, toward”) + custom. More at custom, costume. The noun is from Middle English acustom.

parole.significato: One's dress; what one wears; one's clothes.
parole.testo: The verb is from Middle English atyren, atiren, from Old French atirier (“to equip”), from a- + tire (“rank”), akin to German Zier (“ornament”) and Old Norse tírr (“glory, renown”). The noun is from Middle English atir, from the verb.

parole.significato: The consent of a tenant to the transfer of his relationship to his landlord to another person.
parole.testo: From Old French atorner (“to turn”), through Middle English with the suffix -ment.
From Middle English consenter, consentour, from Old French consenteor and partly from Middle English consenten; equivalent to consent + -er.
From a convergence of Middle English corour, currour, from Old French coreor, agent noun of corir (“to run”), and Middle English courier, a borrowing of Middle French courrier, from Italian corriere.

parole.significato: A company, business, organization, or other purposeful endeavor.
parole.testo: From Old French via Middle English and Middle French entreprise, feminine past participle of entreprendre (“to undertake”), from entre (“in between”) + prendre (“to take”), from Latin inter + prehendō, see prehensile.

parole.significato: To repossess a mortgaged property whose owner has failed to make the necessary payments; used with on.
parole.testo: Partially from Middle English foreclosen, forclosen, from Old French forclos, past participle of forclore (“to exclude”), from for- (“(prefix used to express error, exclusion, or inadequacy)”) + clore (“to shut”), and partially from Middle English forclusen (“to close up”), from Old English forclȳsa

parole.significato: To exclude, oust, or dispossess by a judgment; prohibit (from).
parole.testo: From Middle English forjugen; in sense 1, from Old French fourjugier (“to judge illegally, dispossess”); in sense 2, from Middle English for- + jugen (“to judge”), equivalent to for- + judge. Compare fordeem.

parole.significato: A trick; a device or instrument.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle English gin, ginne (“cleverness, scheme, talent, device, machine”), from Old French gin, an aphetism of Old French engin (“engine”); and partly from Middle English grin, grine (“snare, trick, stratagem, deceit, temptation, noose, halter, instrument”), from Old English grin, gryn,

parole.significato: The state or property of being haughty; arrogance, snobbery.
parole.testo: From Middle English hauteynesse, hautenesse, from Middle English hautein (“proud, haughty”), from Old French hautain + Middle English -nesse. Reanalysed in Modern English as haughty + -ness.

parole.significato: Expending or bestowing profusely; profuse; prodigal.
parole.testo: From Middle English laves, lavas, lavage (“extravagant, wasteful, prodigal”), from lavas (“excessive abundance”), from Old French lavasse, lavache (“torrent of rain”); possibly later conflated in some senses by Middle English laven (“to pour out”), equivalent to lave + -ish. Compare Scots lawage, la

parole.significato: Having the color of marigolds, a bright yellowish-orange hue.
parole.testo: From Middle English marigolde, marygoldye, from Mary (referring to the Virgin Mary) + Middle English golde (“marigold”).
From Old French quisse (“thigh”), perhaps via Middle English quishete; compare cuisset (extended form of cuisse), and quish (variant form of cuisse).

parole.significato: A longitudinal channel, groove, or recess cut out of the edge or face of a plank of wood or other material; especially,…
parole.testo: From Middle English rabeten, from Old French raboter, rabouter (“to thrust back”, verb), from Old French re- + boter, bouter. Doublet of rebut. The noun is from Middle English rabet, from Old French rabot, from the verb.
From Middle English singler, from Old French sangler, seingler, sengler (“single, individual”) and a shortened form of Middle English singuler.

parole.significato: An action that is intended to cause, or actually causes, delay.
parole.testo: From Middle English stallen (“to abide, dwell, place in a location, stop, come to a standstill”), partly from Old French estaler, ultimately from the same origin as Etymology 1 (see above); and partly from Middle English stalle (“fixed position, stall”).

parole.significato: Also used with the impersonal pronoun it (dated): to shirk or wander from business or duty; (specifically) of a student…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English truaunten (“to obtain alms fraudulently; to behave like a rogue or scoundrel; to neglect a duty; to be idle or lazy”), and then partly: * from Old French truander (modern French truander (“to cheat, to con”)), from truand (noun) (see etymology 1) + -er (suffix forming i
